q: Which gas was absent, or present only in traces, in the primitive atmosphere of the Earth?
o: Free oxygen
Methane
Ammonia
Water vapour
x: The early atmosphere was reducing: it had methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour but little or no free oxygen. Free oxygen built up only after photosynthetic organisms appeared.

q: Which mixture of gases did Miller and Urey circulate in their apparatus to imitate the early atmosphere?
o: Oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide and water vapour
Methane, oxygen, hydrogen and ozone
Ammonia, oxygen, carbon monoxide and argon
Methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour
x: Miller and Urey used methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour, the gases thought to make up the reducing early atmosphere. Mixtures with oxygen or ozone do not match early-Earth conditions.

q: In the Miller–Urey experiment, the electric sparks passed through the gases represented:
o: Lightning in the early atmosphere
Ultraviolet light from the Sun
Heat from volcanoes
Radioactive decay in rocks
x: The sparks between electrodes imitated lightning, one of the main energy sources on the early Earth. Ultraviolet light and volcanic heat were also energy sources, but they were not what the sparks stood for.

q: After running for about a week, the Miller–Urey apparatus was found to contain:
o: Complete functional proteins
Simple amino acids such as glycine and alanine
Molecules of DNA
Living bacterial cells
x: The water collected simple organic molecules, especially amino acids like glycine and alanine. No proteins, DNA or living cells were formed; the experiment showed only the first step of chemical evolution.

q: The hypothesis that life arose on Earth by gradual chemical evolution in a reducing atmosphere was proposed independently by:
o: Miller and Urey
Darwin and Wallace
Oparin and Haldane
Lamarck and Weismann
x: A. I. Oparin (Russia) and J. B. S. Haldane (Britain) proposed this independently in the 1920s. Miller and Urey later tested it experimentally in 1953.

q: Oparin called the tiny droplets formed when organic polymers cluster together in water:
o: Nucleoids
Ribosomes
Mesosomes
Coacervates
x: Coacervates are colloidal droplets of organic molecules surrounded by a boundary of water molecules. Oparin suggested that such droplets were forerunners of the first cells.

q: Haldane described the early oceans, in which organic molecules collected over millions of years, as a:
o: Concentrated ozone layer
Oxidising sea
Coacervate membrane
Hot dilute soup
x: Haldane called the early ocean a 'hot dilute soup' of organic compounds (the primordial soup). There was no ozone layer then, and the sea was not oxidising because free oxygen was absent.

q: Why can organic molecules not build up in today's oceans the way they did on the early Earth?
o: Free oxygen breaks them down and living microbes consume them
Today's oceans are too cold for any reactions
The ozone layer produces too much ultraviolet light
Today's oceans contain no dissolved salts
x: Today free oxygen oxidises organic molecules and microorganisms quickly use them as food. On the early Earth neither oxygen nor living organisms were present, so the molecules could accumulate.

q: Strong ultraviolet radiation could reach the surface of the early Earth mainly because:
o: The Sun was much closer to the Earth
No ozone layer had yet formed
The atmosphere was rich in oxygen
Thick clouds focused the sunlight
x: Ozone forms from oxygen, and the early atmosphere had little free oxygen, so there was no ozone layer to absorb ultraviolet rays. This UV was one energy source for forming organic molecules.

q: Which of the following was NOT an energy source for chemical evolution on the early Earth?
o: Lightning discharges
Ultraviolet radiation from the Sun
Heat from volcanic activity
Energy released by aerobic respiration
x: Lightning, ultraviolet radiation and volcanic heat supplied energy for joining simple molecules. Aerobic respiration needs living cells and free oxygen, neither of which existed at that stage.

q: The primitive atmosphere is described as 'reducing' because it:
o: Contained large amounts of free oxygen
Contained hydrogen-rich gases and little or no free oxygen
Had a thick protective ozone layer
Was made only of nitrogen and argon
x: A reducing atmosphere is rich in hydrogen and hydrogen-containing gases such as methane and ammonia, with almost no free oxygen. Such conditions allow organic molecules to form and remain stable.

q: Which is the correct order of steps in chemical evolution leading to the first cells?
o: Inorganic gases, then polymers, then simple organic monomers, then cells, then coacervate-like droplets
Simple organic monomers, then inorganic gases, then coacervate-like droplets, then polymers, then cells
Coacervate-like droplets, then inorganic gases, then polymers, then simple organic monomers, then cells
Inorganic gases, then simple organic monomers, then polymers, then coacervate-like droplets, then cells
x: Simple gases first formed small organic monomers (amino acids, sugars, bases), which joined into polymers. Polymers gathered into droplets with a boundary, and these gave rise to the first cells.

q: Clay surfaces are thought to have helped chemical evolution on the early Earth by:
o: Releasing free oxygen into the atmosphere
Supplying ATP to the first cells
Blocking lightning from reaching the oceans
Concentrating monomers and catalysing their joining into polymers
x: Clay particles can hold monomers such as amino acids close together and act as catalysts, helping them link into polymers. They did not release oxygen or provide ATP.

q: According to the Oparin–Haldane hypothesis, the first living cells were:
o: Aerobic autotrophic eukaryotes
Anaerobic heterotrophic prokaryotes
Anaerobic autotrophic eukaryotes
Aerobic heterotrophic eukaryotes
x: Oparin and Haldane proposed that the first cells were simple prokaryotes that fed on the organic molecules of the primordial soup (heterotrophs) without using oxygen (anaerobes), since no free oxygen existed.

q: The free oxygen of the Earth's atmosphere came mainly from:
o: Gases released by volcanic eruptions
Lightning splitting nitrogen molecules
Respiration by early heterotrophs
Photosynthesis by early cyanobacteria
x: Photosynthetic prokaryotes such as cyanobacteria released oxygen as a by-product of splitting water. Over a very long time this changed the atmosphere from reducing to oxidising.

q: When free oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere, which consequence followed?
o: An ozone layer formed and aerobic respiration became possible
Abiotic formation of organic molecules became faster
All anaerobic organisms became extinct
Methane and ammonia in the air increased
x: Oxygen formed the ozone layer, which cut down ultraviolet radiation, and allowed organisms to evolve aerobic respiration. Oxygen actually stopped further abiotic synthesis, and anaerobes still survive in oxygen-free places.

q: The main importance of the Miller–Urey experiment is that it showed:
o: Living cells can arise in a few days from non-living matter
Life arises spontaneously from decaying meat
The early atmosphere contained abundant oxygen
Organic molecules can form from inorganic gases under early-Earth conditions
x: The experiment supported the Oparin–Haldane idea by producing amino acids from simple gases and energy. It did not produce cells, and it used an oxygen-free gas mixture.

q: In which year did Stanley Miller carry out his experiment on the origin of organic molecules?
x: Miller, working with Harold Urey, did the experiment in 1953. The other years belong to Darwin's Origin of Species (1859), Oparin's proposal (1924) and Lamarck's book (1809).

q: In the Miller–Urey apparatus, the flask of boiling water represented:
o: The primitive atmosphere
The primitive ocean
Lightning
The ozone layer
x: Boiling water in the lower flask stood for the early ocean and supplied water vapour. The gases in the spark chamber represented the atmosphere, and the sparks represented lightning.

q: What was the role of the condenser in the Miller–Urey apparatus?
o: It cooled the vapours so that water and products fell back, like rain
It supplied energy, like lightning
It removed oxygen from the gases
It heated the water to form vapour
x: The condenser cooled the hot gases so water and the newly formed molecules condensed and collected below, imitating rain carrying compounds into the sea. The electrodes, not the condenser, supplied energy.

q: Miller sterilised and sealed his apparatus before the experiment. Why was this necessary?
o: To let free oxygen enter the system
To make sure the organic molecules came from the gases, not from living contaminants
To kill the amino acids after they formed
To increase the voltage of the sparks
x: Sterilising and sealing ruled out microbes or outside organic matter, so any amino acids found must have formed from the gas mixture. Letting in oxygen would have spoiled the reducing conditions.

q: Coacervates are considered important in the origin of life because they:
o: Contained DNA and ribosomes like modern cells
Had a boundary separating their internal chemistry from the surroundings
Could carry out photosynthesis
Were true living cells able to reproduce exactly
x: A coacervate has an outer boundary, so it can keep a different internal chemistry and take in substances, much like a primitive membrane. It lacks DNA and ribosomes and is not a true cell.

q: Coacervates are formed by:
o: Division of bacterial cells
Clustering of organic polymers in water into droplets
Crystallisation of salts from sea water
Freezing of water vapour in the atmosphere
x: When organic polymers such as proteins and other large molecules are mixed in water, they come together into stable droplets called coacervates. They do not arise from living cells or from salt crystals.

q: Why is RNA, rather than DNA, thought to have been the first hereditary molecule?
o: RNA is double-stranded and more stable than DNA
RNA contains thymine instead of uracil
RNA can only be made inside living cells
RNA can store genetic information and also catalyse reactions
x: Some RNA molecules (ribozymes) act as enzymes and can also carry information, so RNA could both copy itself and speed up reactions. RNA is usually single-stranded, less stable than DNA, and contains uracil, not thymine.

q: How does the concept of chemical evolution differ from the old idea of spontaneous generation?
o: It says living things still arise from mud and meat every day
It says life on Earth was brought from another planet
It says life arose very slowly from simple molecules under early-Earth conditions that no longer exist
It says life has always come only from pre-existing cells
x: Spontaneous generation claimed organisms such as maggots arise quickly from non-living matter today. Chemical evolution proposes a single, very slow origin of life from molecules under the special conditions of the early Earth.

q: The Earth is estimated to be about how old?
o: 4.6 billion years
4.6 million years
460 million years
46 billion years
x: Radioactive dating of rocks and meteorites shows the Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago. Life appeared roughly a billion years after that.

q: The oldest fossil evidence of cells, from prokaryote-like organisms, is about how old?
o: 350 million years
35 million years
4.6 billion years
3.5 billion years
x: Fossil prokaryotes and stromatolites date back about 3.5 billion years. 4.6 billion years is the age of the Earth itself, when no life existed.

q: Which is the correct order in which these groups appeared on Earth?
o: Eukaryotes, photosynthetic prokaryotes, anaerobic prokaryotes
Photosynthetic prokaryotes, eukaryotes, anaerobic prokaryotes
Anaerobic prokaryotes, photosynthetic prokaryotes, eukaryotes
Anaerobic prokaryotes, eukaryotes, photosynthetic prokaryotes
x: The first cells were anaerobic prokaryotes. Photosynthetic prokaryotes then added oxygen to the atmosphere, and the larger, more complex eukaryotic cells appeared much later.

q: If Miller had added a large amount of free oxygen to his gas mixture, what result would be expected?
o: Many more amino acids, because oxygen speeds up their synthesis
Living cells, because oxygen allows respiration
No change, because oxygen takes no part in such reactions
Far fewer organic molecules, because oxygen oxidises and breaks them down
x: Organic molecules form and survive best in a reducing atmosphere. Oxygen oxidises them, so the yield would fall. This is why an oxygen-free early atmosphere was essential to the hypothesis.

q: The first proteins and the first nucleic acids were formed by joining, respectively:
o: Amino acids and nucleotides
Nucleotides and amino acids
Fatty acids and glucose
Glycerol and amino acids
x: Proteins are polymers of amino acids, and nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides. Fatty acids and glycerol make lipids, and glucose makes polysaccharides.

q: Which property must a protocell gain before it can be called a living cell?
o: A spherical shape
A watery interior
The ability to reproduce and pass on hereditary information
The ability to absorb light
x: Many non-living droplets are spherical, contain water and may absorb light. Being alive requires the ability to reproduce and pass on information to offspring, along with metabolism.

q: Which statement is NOT part of the Oparin–Haldane hypothesis?
o: The first organisms were aerobic photosynthetic cells
Life arose on Earth from non-living chemicals
The primitive atmosphere was reducing
Lightning and ultraviolet light supplied energy for synthesis
x: The hypothesis held that life arose locally from chemicals in a reducing atmosphere, powered by lightning and UV. It proposed that the first organisms were anaerobic heterotrophs, not aerobic photosynthesisers.

q: Lamarck put forward his theory of evolution in his book Philosophie Zoologique, published in:
x: Lamarck published Philosophie Zoologique in 1809, the year Darwin was born. 1859 is the year of Darwin's Origin of Species.

q: Lamarck's theory of evolution is commonly known as the theory of:
o: Natural selection
Germplasm
Inheritance of acquired characters
Chemical evolution
x: Lamarckism is the theory of inheritance of acquired characters. Natural selection is Darwin's theory, and the germplasm theory is Weismann's.

q: Which statement correctly describes Lamarck's principle of use and disuse?
o: Organs change only through random mutations
Organs used often become larger and stronger, while unused organs weaken and may disappear
Organs are reduced only by natural selection acting on variation
The size of every organ is fixed at birth and cannot change
x: Lamarck held that continued use develops an organ and long disuse makes it shrink and finally vanish. Mutation and natural selection are later and Darwinian ideas, not Lamarck's.

q: According to Lamarck, the giraffe has a long neck because:
o: Ancestors born with longer necks survived and reproduced more
A sudden mutation produced a long neck in a single generation
Its ancestors stretched their necks to reach high leaves, and the extra length was inherited
Short-necked giraffes were hunted out by humans
x: Lamarck said the neck grew by stretching (use) and this acquired length was passed to offspring. Survival of naturally long-necked individuals is the Darwinian explanation.

q: Lamarck explained the absence of legs in snakes as the result of:
o: Natural selection of legless mutants
Removal of the legs by predators
Snake ancestors never having had legs
Disuse of the legs over many generations, with the loss being inherited
x: Lamarck argued that ancestors of snakes crawled through narrow spaces, stopped using their legs, and the reduced legs were passed on until they vanished. Selection of mutants is a Darwinian or modern view.

q: The phrase 'inheritance of acquired characters' means that:
o: Traits gained during an organism's lifetime are passed on to its offspring
Traits present at birth are passed to offspring
Only dominant traits are passed to offspring
Traits are inherited only from the mother
x: An acquired character is one developed during life, such as muscle built by exercise. Lamarck claimed such traits are passed on; inheritance of inborn traits is ordinary heredity.

q: Which of the following is an acquired character?
o: Blood group A received from a parent
Red–green colour blindness
Brown eye colour
Large arm muscles developed by a blacksmith through hard work
x: The blacksmith's muscles are developed during life by use, so they are acquired. Blood group, colour blindness and eye colour are controlled by genes received from parents.

q: From his mouse-tail experiment, Weismann concluded that:
o: Acquired characters are inherited after enough generations
Use and disuse controls the length of the tail
Changes in body cells are not passed on to the offspring
Injury to the body causes mutations in the gametes
x: Cutting tails changed only the body (somatic) cells; the germ cells were unaffected, so offspring had normal tails. This was strong evidence against the inheritance of acquired characters.

q: Weismann cut off the tails of mice for many successive generations. What was the result?
o: Every generation was born with tails of normal length
The tails became a little shorter in each generation
Tailless mice appeared after a few generations
Half of each litter was born without tails
x: Despite repeated cutting for many generations, every new litter had normal tails. The loss of the tail was an acquired character and was never inherited.

q: According to Weismann's germplasm theory, only changes in which cells can be inherited?
o: Muscle cells
Germ cells
Skin cells
Nerve cells
x: Weismann distinguished germ plasm (reproductive cells) from somatoplasm (body cells). Only changes in germ cells reach the next generation.

q: Why does modern genetics reject Lamarck's mechanism of evolution?
o: The environment never affects the body of an organism
Organs cannot change in size however much they are used
Changes in body cells do not alter the DNA of the gametes, so they cannot be transmitted
Acquired changes are transmitted only by the female parent
x: Inherited traits pass through the genes in gametes. Exercise or injury changes body cells but not the DNA of eggs or sperm. Use can enlarge an organ in an individual, but that change is not inherited.

q: For centuries some communities have pierced the ears of their children, yet babies are still born without holes in their ears. This observation argues against:
o: Inheritance of acquired characters
Natural selection
The germplasm theory
Chemical evolution
x: Ear holes are acquired during life. If acquired characters were inherited, babies would eventually be born with them. The observation actually supports the germplasm theory.

q: Lamarck proposed that changes in an organism's body begin in response to:
o: Random mutations in its genes
Selection of mates by the organism
Choice of parents by animal breeders
New needs created by changes in the environment
x: Lamarck said a changing environment creates new needs, which change the animal's habits and so the use of its organs. Random mutation and selection belong to Darwinian and modern theory.

q: Which statement about Lamarck is correct?
o: He was among the first to propose that species change over time in response to the environment
He first proposed the theory of natural selection
He proved by experiment that acquired characters are inherited
He believed that species are fixed and never change
x: Lamarck rejected the idea of fixed species and proposed a full theory of gradual change. His mechanism was never proved; natural selection was proposed later by Darwin and Wallace.

q: The two central postulates of Lamarckism are:
o: Overproduction, and struggle for existence
Variation, and survival of the fittest
Mutation, and genetic drift
Use and disuse, and inheritance of acquired characters
x: Lamarck's theory rests on use and disuse of organs and on inheritance of the resulting changes. Overproduction, struggle, variation and survival of the fittest are Darwin's postulates.

q: A weightlifter develops very large muscles by training. According to Lamarck's theory, his children would be:
o: Born with ordinary muscles, because acquired traits are not inherited
Born with weaker muscles because of disuse
Born with larger than usual muscles
Unaffected unless the trait was on the Y chromosome
x: Lamarck held that a trait acquired by use is passed to the next generation, so he would predict stronger-muscled children. Modern genetics predicts ordinary muscles, but the question asks for Lamarck's view.

q: Which is a key difference between the theories of Lamarck and Darwin?
o: Darwin said change arises in individuals during life in response to need; Lamarck said existing variation is selected
Both said that acquired characters can never be inherited
Lamarck accepted natural selection, but Darwin rejected it
Lamarck said change arises in individuals during life in response to need; Darwin said existing variation is selected
x: For Lamarck, each organism changes itself through use or disuse and passes the change on. For Darwin, individuals already vary, and nature selects the favourable variations.

q: Which result, if it had been observed, would have supported Lamarck's theory?
o: Offspring of mice whose tails were cut being born with normal tails
Offspring of mice whose tails were cut being born with shorter tails
Dark moths becoming common on soot-covered trees
Resistant bacteria surviving an antibiotic
x: Lamarck predicted that an acquired change, such as a shortened tail, would be inherited. Weismann actually found normal tails. Moths and bacteria are examples of natural selection.

q: Lamarck would explain the small, almost functionless vermiform appendix in humans as the result of:
o: Disuse over many generations
Overproduction of offspring
Struggle for existence
Changes in the germ plasm
x: In Lamarck's view an organ that is not used shrinks, and the reduction is inherited, so a vestigial organ reflects long disuse. Overproduction and struggle are Darwinian ideas.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of Lamarck's propositions?
o: Internal vital force
Effect of environment and new needs
Struggle for existence
Use and disuse of organs
x: Lamarck's propositions were an internal vital force, the effect of environment and new needs, use and disuse, and inheritance of acquired characters. Struggle for existence is part of Darwin's theory.

q: Weismann proposed that hereditary information passes:
o: From body cells to germ cells, but not from germ cells to body cells
Freely in both directions between body and germ cells
Only between body cells and never to germ cells
From germ cells to body cells, but not from body cells to germ cells
x: The germ line produces both the next germ cells and the body cells, but changes in body cells do not flow back to the germ cells (the Weismann barrier). This is why acquired traits are not inherited.

q: The first organised theory of evolution was proposed by:
o: Darwin
Wallace
Lamarck
Weismann
x: Lamarck's theory (1809) came about fifty years before Darwin and Wallace proposed natural selection. Weismann later tested Lamarck's ideas experimentally.

q: Which part of Lamarck's theory is actually true within the life of a single individual?
o: Regular use can make an organ stronger
Acquired characters are passed to offspring
New organs appear in one generation because of need
Disuse produces a new species at once
x: Exercise really does strengthen muscles in the person who exercises. What fails is the next step: such acquired changes are not passed on to children.

q: Which is the correct order of events in Lamarck's reasoning?
o: New needs, change in environment, inheritance of the change, change in use of organs, change in organs
Change in environment, new needs, change in use of organs, change in organs, inheritance of the change
Change in organs, change in environment, new needs, inheritance of the change, change in use of organs
Inheritance of the change, change in use of organs, new needs, change in environment, change in organs
x: Lamarck argued that a changed environment creates new needs, which alter habits and the use of organs. Organs then grow or shrink, and this change is inherited by the offspring.

q: Lamarck and Darwin both agreed that:
o: Variations are caused by mutations in genes
Natural selection is the main cause of evolution
Species are not fixed and change gradually over generations
Species were created in their present form
x: Both rejected fixed species and saw evolution as gradual change over generations. They disagreed on the mechanism; mutation as a source of variation was discovered after both of them.

q: Weismann's mouse-tail experiment was designed mainly to test which Lamarckian idea?
o: Internal vital force
Effect of new needs
Inheritance of acquired characters
Origin of life from chemicals
x: Weismann removed tails (an acquired change) and checked whether the offspring inherited it. The experiment tested whether acquired characters are inherited, and the answer was no.

q: A gardener has trimmed a hedge into a box shape every year for 30 years. Seeds from this hedge will grow into plants that are:
o: Of the natural shape of the species
Box-shaped like the parent hedge
Smaller in every part
Unable to produce leaves
x: Trimming is an acquired change in body tissues and does not affect the genes in the seeds. The young plants grow into the normal shape of the species.

q: Which statement would Lamarck have agreed with?
o: Variation is random, and only the best-suited individuals survive
Changes in body cells cannot affect the gametes
Species are fixed and do not change
An organism passes to its offspring changes it acquired during its life
x: Inheritance of acquired characters was the core of Lamarck's theory. Random variation with selection is Darwin's idea, and the barrier between body and gametes is Weismann's.

q: In Weismann's theory, the term somatoplasm refers to:
o: The germ cells that form gametes
The nucleus of the egg cell
The body cells, whose changes die with the individual
The cytoplasm of the sperm
x: Weismann divided the organism into germ plasm (reproductive cells) and somatoplasm (all other body cells). Changes in somatoplasm are not passed to the next generation.

q: In Lamarck's giraffe explanation, which step does modern genetics reject?
o: Giraffes stretched their necks to reach leaves
The food of giraffes was high on trees
The extra neck length gained by stretching was passed to offspring
Neck muscles may strengthen with use
x: Stretching, high food and strengthening by use are all reasonable. The rejected step is the inheritance of the acquired length, because body changes do not alter genes in the gametes.

q: Which example did Lamarck use to illustrate his theory?
o: The peppered moth in industrial England
The finches of the Galápagos Islands
The long neck of the giraffe
Antibiotic resistance in bacteria
x: The giraffe's neck is Lamarck's classic example of use and inheritance of acquired characters. The moth, finches and resistant bacteria are examples used for natural selection.

q: Darwin's book On the Origin of Species was published in:
x: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection appeared in 1859. In 1858 the joint Darwin–Wallace papers were presented; 1809 is Lamarck's book.

q: Darwin collected much of the evidence for his theory during a voyage around the world on the ship:
o: HMS Endeavour
HMS Beagle
HMS Victory
HMS Bounty
x: Darwin sailed as a naturalist on HMS Beagle (1831–1836), visiting South America and the Galápagos Islands, among other places.

q: Darwin's finches, a group of related birds with beaks suited to different foods, were studied on the:
o: Malay Archipelago
Galápagos Islands
Canary Islands
Andaman Islands
x: Darwin observed these finches on the Galápagos Islands off Ecuador. The Malay Archipelago is where Wallace worked.

q: Alfred Russel Wallace is important in the history of evolution because he:
o: Disproved the theory of natural selection
Performed the mouse-tail experiment
Independently arrived at the theory of natural selection
Proposed the inheritance of acquired characters
x: Working in the Malay Archipelago, Wallace reached the same idea as Darwin and sent him an essay in 1858. The mouse-tail experiment was Weismann's, and acquired characters were Lamarck's idea.

q: Darwin's idea of the struggle for existence was influenced by Malthus, who argued that:
o: The Earth is very old and changes slowly
Acquired characters are inherited
Populations tend to increase faster than their food supply
Species are fixed and unchanging
x: Malthus wrote that populations grow geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically, so there must be competition and death. The idea of a very old, slowly changing Earth came from Lyell.

q: From Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology, Darwin took the idea that:
o: Populations grow faster than their food supply
Survival of the fittest decides evolution
The Earth is very old and is changed by slow, gradual processes
Changes in body cells are not inherited
x: Lyell showed that slow geological processes acting over vast time shape the Earth, giving Darwin the long time-scale his theory needed. The population idea came from Malthus.

q: The phrase 'survival of the fittest' was first used by:
o: Charles Darwin
Thomas Malthus
Herbert Spencer
Alfred Wallace
x: Herbert Spencer coined the phrase after reading Darwin's work; Darwin later used it as another name for natural selection. Malthus wrote on population growth.

q: A single cod fish lays millions of eggs each year, yet the number of cod in the sea stays roughly constant. This illustrates:
o: Inheritance of acquired characters
Use and disuse of organs
Overproduction followed by a struggle for existence
Chemical evolution
x: Organisms produce far more offspring than can survive, so most die in the competition for food and space and from predators. This is the basis of Darwin's struggle for existence.

q: According to Darwin, the struggle for existence is most severe between:
o: Members of different species
Members of the same species
Organisms and the climate
Producers and decomposers
x: Individuals of the same species need the same food, space and mates, so competition among them (intraspecific struggle) is the most intense.

q: A cactus surviving a long drought in the desert is an example of which kind of struggle?
o: Struggle with the environment
Intraspecific struggle
Interspecific struggle
Artificial selection
x: Darwin described three kinds of struggle: within a species, between species, and against physical conditions. Surviving drought is a struggle against the environment.

q: Which kind of variation is important for evolution according to Darwin's theory?
o: Variation that can be inherited
Variation caused by injury
Variation produced by exercise
Variation that appears only in old age
x: Only heritable variations can be passed on, so only they can accumulate over generations. Changes caused by injury or exercise are acquired and are not inherited.

q: A major gap in Darwin's original theory was that he:
o: Did not notice variation among individuals
Ignored the struggle for existence
Could not explain how variations arise and are inherited
Believed that species were fixed
x: Darwin knew variation existed but not its cause or how it was inherited, as Mendel's work and genes were unknown to him. Genetics and mutation later filled this gap.

q: The modern synthetic theory (Neo-Darwinism) improved Darwin's theory mainly by adding:
o: Inheritance of acquired characters
Genetics and mutation as the sources of heritable variation
Use and disuse of organs
Spontaneous generation of life
x: Neo-Darwinism combines natural selection with Mendelian genetics, mutation and recombination, which explain where variation comes from. Lamarckian ideas were not added.

q: In industrial areas of England in the 1800s, the dark form of the peppered moth became common because:
o: Dark moths on soot-darkened tree trunks were harder for birds to see, so more survived and bred
Soot on the trunks turned the light moths dark
Dark moths were stronger fliers than light moths
Light moths deliberately moved to the countryside
x: Soot killed lichens and darkened tree bark, so light moths stood out and were eaten by birds. Dark moths survived and reproduced more, so the dark form spread. Soot did not change the colour of any moth.

q: After air pollution in England was reduced, the light form of the peppered moth became common again. This shows that:
o: Moths can change their colour at will
Pollution increases the mutation rate of moths
Acquired characters are inherited
Natural selection favours whichever variation suits the current environment
x: When tree trunks became light again, light moths were better camouflaged and bird predation reversed. Which trait is 'fit' depends on the environment at the time.

q: In the peppered moth example, the selecting agent was:
o: Soot in the air
Insect-eating birds
Lichens on the trees
Factory workers
x: Birds that hunt by sight ate the moths that were easier to see. Soot and lichens changed the background, but predation by birds did the selecting.

q: When an antibiotic is used against a bacterial population, resistant bacteria increase in number because:
o: The antibiotic causes the bacteria to become resistant
The bacteria learn to avoid the antibiotic
The antibiotic supplies energy to the bacteria
A few bacteria already carried resistance, survived and multiplied
x: Resistance arises by chance mutation before the drug is used. The antibiotic kills the sensitive bacteria, and the resistant ones survive and multiply. The drug selects resistance; it does not create it.

q: A patient stops a prescribed course of antibiotics early. Why can this encourage antibiotic resistance?
o: The least sensitive bacteria survive and multiply, so the surviving population is more resistant
The antibiotic itself turns into resistant bacteria
The patient's immune system makes bacteria resistant
Stopping early changes the patient's genes
x: A short course kills mainly the most sensitive bacteria. The more resistant ones that survive go on to multiply, so selection shifts the population towards resistance.

q: Repeated spraying of DDT led to DDT-resistant houseflies. In Darwinian terms, DDT acted as:
o: A selection pressure
A source of acquired characters
A cause of use and disuse
A source of new energy
x: DDT killed the susceptible flies, leaving the few naturally resistant ones to breed. It acted as a selection pressure that favoured resistance.

q: Darwin concluded that the different finch species of the Galápagos Islands had:
o: Been created separately on each island
Changed their beaks by using them more
All eaten the same kind of food
Descended from a common ancestor and become adapted to different foods
x: Darwin proposed that one ancestral finch species gave rise to several species whose beaks became suited to seeds, insects or other foods. Changing beaks by use is a Lamarckian idea.

q: Darwin used the work of pigeon breeders as evidence that:
o: Selection over many generations can produce large changes in a species
Acquired characters are inherited
Species never change
New species appear in a single generation
x: Breeders produced very different pigeon varieties by choosing which birds bred. Darwin argued that nature could select in a similar way over far longer time.

q: The main difference between artificial and natural selection is that in artificial selection:
o: No variation is needed
Acquired characters are inherited
Change happens within a single generation
Humans choose which individuals breed
x: In artificial selection humans pick the parents for traits they want; in natural selection the environment decides who survives and breeds. Both need heritable variation.

q: In Darwinian terms, the 'fittest' individual is the one that:
o: Is physically the strongest
Leaves the most surviving, fertile offspring
Lives the longest
Is the largest in size
x: Darwinian fitness means reproductive success. A strong or long-lived individual that leaves few offspring contributes little to the next generation.

q: Which statement about natural selection is correct?
o: Individuals evolve new traits during their lifetime when they need them
Individuals are selected, but it is populations that evolve over generations
Natural selection creates new variations as they are needed
Natural selection works towards a planned goal of perfection
x: Selection decides which individuals survive and breed, but an individual's genes do not change; the make-up of the population changes over generations. Selection only acts on variation that already exists.

q: Which is the correct order of steps in Darwin's theory?
o: Struggle for existence, overproduction, origin of new species, survival of the fittest, inheritance of favourable variations
Overproduction, struggle for existence, survival of the fittest, inheritance of favourable variations, origin of new species
Survival of the fittest, overproduction, inheritance of favourable variations, struggle for existence, origin of new species
Origin of new species, inheritance of favourable variations, struggle for existence, overproduction, survival of the fittest
x: Overproduction leads to a struggle for existence; individuals with favourable variations survive and pass them on; over many generations these build up to form new species.

q: According to Darwin, the long neck of the giraffe evolved because:
o: Giraffes stretched their necks and passed the extra length to their young
Giraffes with naturally longer necks reached more food, survived and passed on the trait
A single mutation produced long necks in all giraffes at once
All giraffes stretched their necks equally
x: Darwin said neck length varied naturally; longer-necked individuals got more food in hard times, survived and bred more. Stretching and passing on the gain is Lamarck's explanation.

q: Darwin observed that although organisms produce many offspring, natural populations usually:
o: Double in size every generation
Always decline towards extinction
Remain roughly constant in size over time
Grow without any limit
x: Populations stay fairly stable because food and space are limited and most offspring die. From this Darwin inferred a struggle for existence.

q: According to Darwin, a new species arises by:
o: Sudden appearance in a single generation
Inheritance of characters acquired by use
Gradual accumulation of favourable variations over many generations
Spontaneous generation from non-living matter
x: Darwin saw speciation as slow: small favourable variations are preserved and build up over many generations until the population differs enough to be a new species.

q: In regions where malaria is common, the sickle-cell allele is more frequent than in other regions. This is because:
o: People carrying one sickle-cell allele resist malaria better, so they survive and reproduce more
Malaria parasites cause the sickle-cell mutation in people they infect
People with two sickle-cell alleles are the healthiest
The allele is passed from person to person by mosquito bites
x: Carriers (one normal and one sickle allele) are more resistant to malaria, so natural selection keeps the allele common where malaria occurs. People with two sickle alleles suffer sickle-cell disease.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of Darwin's postulates?
o: Overproduction of offspring
Variation among individuals
Struggle for existence
Inheritance of acquired characters
x: Darwin's theory is built on overproduction, struggle for existence, variation, survival of the fittest and natural selection. Inheritance of acquired characters is Lamarck's idea.

q: Natural selection cannot cause evolution in a population whose members:
o: Show heritable variation
Are all genetically identical
Produce many offspring
Compete for limited food
x: Selection works only by favouring some heritable variants over others. If all individuals are genetically identical, there is nothing to choose between, so the population cannot change by selection.

q: Inherited features that increase an organism's chance of surviving and reproducing in its environment are called:
o: Acquired characters
Adaptations
Vestigial organs
Homologous organs
x: Adaptations are heritable traits that suit an organism to its environment and are built up by natural selection. Acquired characters are gained during life and are not inherited.
